## What Is Local SEO?

Local SEO is the practice of optimizing a business's online presence to attract more customers from relevant local searches. These searches take place on Google and other search engines, map applications, voice assistants, and increasingly, AI-powered local discovery platforms. In 2026, local SEO encompasses a sophisticated ecosystem of signals that determine which businesses appear in local search results, map packs, and AI-generated local recommendations.

According to research from BrightLocal, 98% of consumers used the internet to find information about local businesses in 2025, and 87% of consumers used Google to evaluate local businesses. Local search has become the primary discovery mechanism for businesses with physical locations, service areas, or geographically-defined target markets.

The local search landscape has evolved significantly with the integration of AI. Google's AI Overviews now frequently include local business recommendations, and conversational AI assistants process millions of local intent queries daily. Businesses that invest in local SEO capture high-intent traffic — research shows that 76% of people who search for something nearby on their smartphone visit a related business within 24 hours.

## Google Business Profile: The Foundation of Local SEO

Google Business Profile (GBP, formerly Google My Business) is the single most important element of local SEO. A fully optimized GBP listing directly influences whether your business appears in the Local Pack (the map-based results that appear at the top of local searches), Google Maps results, and Google AI Overview local recommendations.

Complete GBP optimization includes providing accurate and complete business information (name, address, phone number — the "NAP"), selecting the most specific primary and secondary business categories, writing a keyword-rich business description, uploading high-quality photos and videos regularly (businesses with 100+ photos receive 520% more calls than the average), maintaining accurate business hours including special hours for holidays, enabling messaging and booking features, and regularly posting updates, offers, and events through GBP Posts.

### GBP Categories and Attributes

Category selection directly impacts which searches your business appears for. Research from Sterling Sky shows that the primary category is the single most influential ranking factor in local search. Secondary categories add additional visibility for related search terms. Business attributes (wheelchair accessible, free Wi-Fi, outdoor seating, etc.) provide additional matching signals and improve click-through rates by displaying relevant information directly in search results.

## Local Pack Rankings: The Three Pillars

Google's local ranking algorithm evaluates three primary factors, as documented in their official support documentation:

### 1. Relevance

Relevance measures how well a local business listing matches what someone is searching for. Complete and detailed business information helps Google understand your business better and match your listing to relevant searches. Ensuring your GBP categories, description, and services accurately reflect your business is essential for relevance optimization.

### 2. Distance

Distance refers to how far each potential search result is from the location term used in a search. If a user doesn't specify a location, Google calculates distance based on what's known about the user's location. While you can't control distance directly, you can optimize your service area settings and create location-specific content that helps Google associate your business with relevant geographic areas.

### 3. Prominence

Prominence refers to how well-known a business is. This is influenced by link profile, article mentions, review count and quality, local citation consistency, and overall web presence. Prominence is the factor most within your control and where strategic local SEO efforts have the greatest impact.

## Citation Building and NAP Consistency

Local citations are mentions of your business's name, address, and phone number (NAP) across the web. Citations appear on business directories (Yelp, Yellow Pages, BBB), social platforms, industry-specific directories, and data aggregators. Citation consistency is crucial — inconsistent NAP information across different sources confuses search engines and can negatively impact local rankings.

A strategic citation building program targets the most authoritative directories first, ensures 100% consistency in business name formatting, address format, and phone number, and expands to industry-specific and hyper-local directories. Citation management tools automate the process of finding and correcting inconsistencies across hundreds of directory listings.

## Review Management and Reputation

Reviews are a critical local ranking factor and a primary decision-making input for consumers. Research from BrightLocal's Consumer Review Survey shows that 87% of consumers read online reviews for local businesses, and the average consumer reads 10 reviews before feeling able to trust a business.

Effective review management includes actively requesting reviews from satisfied customers (timing requests shortly after positive experiences), responding to all reviews — both positive and negative — promptly and professionally, monitoring reviews across all platforms (Google, Yelp, Facebook, industry-specific sites), and using review insights to identify and address operational issues. Google specifically looks at review recency, velocity (how frequently new reviews are generated), diversity (reviews across multiple platforms), and owner response rate when evaluating local rankings.

## Local Content and Link Building

### Geo-Targeted Content Strategy

Creating content specifically relevant to your local audience signals geographic relevance to search engines. This includes creating location-specific landing pages for each service area, publishing content about local events, news, and community involvement, producing case studies and success stories featuring local clients, and creating "best of" guides and local resource pages that naturally attract local links and engagement.

### Local Link Building

Local links from community organizations, local media, chambers of commerce, business associations, and complementary local businesses provide strong geographic relevance signals. Sponsoring local events, participating in community initiatives, and building relationships with local journalists and bloggers create natural local link opportunities. These links carry double value — they build both domain authority and geographic authority.

## Local SEO for Multi-Location Businesses

Multi-location businesses face unique local SEO challenges including maintaining individual GBP listings for each location, creating unique location-specific content (avoiding duplicate content across location pages), managing reviews and reputation across multiple locations, and implementing local schema markup with location-specific data.

Each location should have its own dedicated landing page with unique content, local testimonials, team photos, directions, and area-specific service information. These pages should use LocalBusiness schema markup with unique identifiers for each location. Research from Moz emphasizes that the quality and uniqueness of location pages directly correlates with local pack visibility.

## Local SEO and AI Search

AI-powered search is transforming local discovery. Google AI Overviews frequently recommend local businesses with conversational context, and AI assistants process millions of "near me" and local intent queries. Optimizing for AI-powered local search requires ensuring your GBP is complete and accurate, having strong review signals, maintaining consistent structured data across all properties, and creating the kind of authoritative, helpful content that AI systems prefer to cite when making local recommendations.

Voice search, which is predominantly local in intent, continues to grow with smart speakers and mobile assistants. Optimizing for natural language queries, featured snippet formats, and FAQ structured data all contribute to visibility in voice-powered local search.

## Measuring Local SEO Performance

Local SEO success measurement includes tracking local pack rankings for target keywords, monitoring GBP insights (views, actions, direction requests, calls), analyzing local organic traffic growth by geographic segment, tracking citation accuracy scores across directories, measuring review velocity and sentiment trends, and monitoring phone call and message volumes from GBP listings.

Attribution remains a challenge in local SEO — many conversions happen offline (phone calls, store visits) after an online discovery. Google's store visit tracking, call tracking, and UTM-tagged GBP links help bridge the online-to-offline attribution gap, providing a more complete picture of local SEO ROI.

# Local SEO in 2026: How to Rank in Google Maps and the Local Pack

May 27, 2026

Category: digital marketing

Published / Last Updated: February 15, 2026Author: Oleg Silin, SEO Specialist & Co-Founder at Mettevo. Oleg has over 10 years of experience managing multi-location search campaigns and overseeing technical optimization for enterprises and SMBs globally.

Disclaimer: This guide discusses local search marketing strategies and mentions the services of Mettevo, an agency providing digital marketing and web development solutions. Independent third-party tools are also evaluated objectively.

---

## TL;DR: Key Takeaways for 2026

- Ranking Pillars: Google's local system weighs three factors — relevance, distance, and prominence. No shortcuts around them.
- The Power of GBP: A fully optimized Google Business Profile, accurately matched to your location and primary category, remains the strongest local signal you can control.
- Citations & Tools: Accurate Name, Address, and Phone (NAP) data across directories is non-negotiable. Tools like BrightLocal, Moz Local, or Whitespark make bulk management realistic.
- Proactive Reviews: Review velocity and sentiment directly impact rankings. Set up an automated request funnel that fires 24–48 hours after service delivery.
- AI Search Resilience: Focus on transactional and navigational keywords to sidestep the informational displacement caused by AI Overviews.

---

Local SEO is the practice of optimizing a business's online presence so it appears in location-based search results — the Google Maps listing, the local pack, and geo-targeted organic results. For businesses that serve customers in a specific area, following proper local SEO guidelines is what separates showing up when someone searches "dentist near me" from being invisible while a competitor two blocks away captures that lead.

This guide covers the full local SEO workflow for 2026: Google Business Profile optimization, citation building, on-page geo-targeting, review strategy, tooling, and how to evaluate whether you need a local SEO agency or can handle it in-house. If you've been burned by vague promises before, you'll find specifics here — not slogans.

«Local SEO is one of those areas where a small business can genuinely compete with larger players — Google's local ranking system weighs proximity and relevance heavily, which means a well-optimized profile and website can outrank a national brand in your own service area. But only if the fundamentals are done right: accurate business data, real reviews, and pages built for the queries your customers actually type.»

> Oleg Silin, SEO Specialist & Co-Founder at Mettevo (source: Superbase)

## What Is Local SEO and How It Differs from Traditional SEO

Local SEO is search engine optimization focused on businesses with a physical location or a defined service area. The goal is visibility in Google's location-based results — the local pack, Google Maps, and geo-modified organic listings. Traditional SEO targets organic blue links across all geographies. Local SEO adds a proximity layer that fundamentally changes how results get ranked and displayed.

The distinction matters because Google treats local queries differently at the algorithm level. According to Google's own documentation, local results are ranked by three factors: relevance (how well a business profile matches the search query), distance (how far the business is from the searcher or from the location term used), and prominence (how well-known and trusted the business is, based on review count, review score, web authority, and other signals). Traditional organic rankings don't use distance as a direct factor. Local rankings do.

That's a big deal in practice. A small law firm in Austin can appear above a national legal directory in the local pack for "personal injury lawyer near me," even though that directory has a far stronger domain. Proximity and profile completeness carry weight in local results that they simply don't carry in standard organic rankings.

"Near me" searches and implicit local intent queries trigger the local pack automatically. Google doesn't require the searcher to type a city name — if the query implies local need (plumber, coffee shop, urgent care), Google uses the device's location to serve local results. This is geo-targeting at the search-engine level, and it means your Google Business Profile and on-page location signals directly determine whether you appear for those high-intent searches. Or, to put it more bluntly: if your GBP is incomplete and your site doesn't mention your city, you're handing those clicks to someone else.

### How Google Ranks Local Results: Map Pack vs. Organic

The Map Pack (also called the local pack or 3-pack) is ranked by Google's local search system using relevance, distance, and prominence. Organic blue links below the Map Pack are ranked by Google's general web ranking systems. These are two separate evaluation processes — a business can rank in one without ranking in the other.

Visually, the Map Pack appears as a map with three business listings directly beneath it. Each listing shows the business name, star rating, address, hours, and a link to the full Google Business Profile. This block sits above standard organic results for most local queries, which makes it the highest-visibility real estate on the page. If you're not in those three spots, you're below the fold for most mobile users.

Algorithmically, Map Pack eligibility depends heavily on Google Business Profile data — categories, attributes, reviews, photos, and NAP accuracy. Organic rankings below the pack depend on traditional signals: page content, backlinks, site speed, and topical authority. I've seen businesses that rank on page one organically but never appear in the Map Pack because their GBP listing was half-finished. The reverse happens too: a well-optimized profile with a weak website can show up in the 3-pack but nowhere in organic results.

Annotated screenshot of a local SERP showing the Map Pack (3-pack) at the top with map, three business listings below the map, local organic results in the middle, and standard organic blue links at the bottom. The Map Pack zone garners the majority of immediate local transactional clicks.

## Google Business Profile Optimization: The Foundation of Local Rankings

A complete and actively managed Google Business Profile is the single most important factor for Map Pack visibility. GBP optimization starts by setting up your Google Business Profile securely, verifying your listing, and then filling every available field — primary category, secondary categories, services, business description with local keywords, attributes, hours, and photos.

Google requires verification before a profile becomes fully visible and editable. Verification methods include video, phone call, and postcard, depending on the business type. Once verified, here's the priority sequence — roughly in order of impact:

1. Primary category selection. This is the strongest signal for which queries trigger your listing. Choose the category that most precisely describes your core business — "personal injury attorney," not just "lawyer." Getting this wrong can mean ranking for the wrong searches entirely.
2. Secondary categories. Add every relevant secondary category. A dental clinic might add "cosmetic dentist," "emergency dental service," and "teeth whitening service." Don't leave these blank — they expand your query footprint.
3. Services and products. List each service individually. Google uses this data to match your profile to specific queries, so vague entries like "general services" don't help.
4. Business description. Write a concise, keyword-informed description. Include your city, service area, and primary services naturally — not as a keyword list. You have 750 characters; use them well.
5. Photos. Google's own documentation confirms that profiles with photos receive more user actions. Upload at least 10 original photos: exterior, interior, team, and service or product images. Stock photos don't count — and customers can tell the difference.
6. Posts. Publish weekly updates — offers, events, new services. Posts signal an active business and give Google fresh content to index. Think of them as mini status updates for your profile.
7. Q&A. Proactively add and answer common questions. This section is indexable and often appears in the profile directly. If you don't populate it, random users might — and their answers won't always be accurate.

### Results From Our Local SEO Work

When we took over local SEO for a multi-location healthcare client, their GBP listings were claimed but barely filled — no secondary categories, two photos, zero posts. Within four months of completing full GBP optimization across all locations, including weekly posting and review response protocols, their Map Pack appearances increased by 68% across target service-area queries. Not overnight, but the trajectory was clear by month two.

For another franchise client with 12 locations, our initial audit revealed that 7 of their 12 GBP listings had incorrect phone numbers inherited from a previous provider. Correcting NAP data alone — no other changes — resulted in a measurable 45% increase in "direction request" actions within six weeks. Sometimes the biggest wins come from fixing what's broken, not adding something new.

### Does Local SEO Work for Service-Area Businesses Without a Storefront?

Yes. Google Business Profile explicitly supports service-area businesses (SABs) — companies that serve customers at their locations rather than from a storefront. SABs can hide their street address on the profile and define up to 20 service areas by city, postal code, or region.

Local pack rankings for SABs still depend on relevance, distance, and prominence — the same factors as storefront businesses. The difference is that Google uses the service area settings and the business's registered address (hidden from public view) to calculate distance. So an SAB based in Dallas can appear in the local pack for "plumber in Dallas" queries, but ranking for "plumber in Houston" from a Dallas address is unlikely without a Houston-area presence. Geography still matters.

Important: Using fake addresses, virtual offices, or keyword-stuffed business names to manipulate geographic eligibility is a policy violation that can result in listing suspension. Google has gotten better at detecting these tactics, and the consequences — losing your listing entirely — far outweigh any short-term gain.

### NAP Consistency and Business Information Accuracy

NAP — Name, Address, Phone number — must be identical across your Google Business Profile, your website, and every external directory where your business is listed. Even minor mismatches (say, "Street" vs. "St." or a different phone format) can create confusion for Google's local systems and dilute your listing's authority.

Google's local ranking relies partly on cross-referencing business data from multiple sources. When the name, address, or phone number on your GBP doesn't match what appears on Yelp, the Better Business Bureau, or your own website's footer, Google's confidence in your business data drops. This doesn't trigger a formal penalty — Google hasn't documented a manual or algorithmic penalty specifically for NAP mismatches — but inconsistent data weakens the prominence signal that feeds local rankings. Think of it as noise that makes it harder for Google to trust your information.

The most common cause of NAP inconsistency? A business changes its address or phone number without updating all directories. Old listings persist, and Google's crawlers find conflicting data. The fix is a full citation audit: identify every directory where your business appears and make sure every entry matches your current, canonical NAP exactly. It's tedious work, but it's foundational.

### Leveraging Reviews to Strengthen Your Profile

Review quantity, recency, and sentiment are confirmed local ranking signals under Google's prominence factor. More reviews with higher average ratings correlate with better Map Pack positions — Google's documentation explicitly states that review count and score influence local prominence. But beyond rankings, reviews shape whether a searcher actually clicks on your listing or scrolls past it.

Strategies that work within Google's review policies involve creating a systemic feedback loop. The best approach is multi-channel:

- Email funnel: Trigger an automated review request via email 24 to 48 hours after the service is rendered, while the positive experience is fresh. Timing matters more than most people realize.
- SMS reminders: Text messages have higher open rates than email. A polite follow-up a few hours after a local purchase often yields quick 5-star ratings.
- Physical triggers: Place QR codes on receipts, lobby desks, or table tents (for restaurants) linking directly to your Google review page. Make it effortless.

You must respond to every review — positive and negative. Negative reviews shouldn't be ignored; replying with empathy transforms a poor rating into a demonstration of customer care. For instance: "Hi [Name], we sincerely apologize that the wait time exceeded your expectations. We'd love to make this right — please reach out to our manager at [Phone/Email]." That response isn't just for the unhappy customer. It's for every future prospect reading your reviews.

Velocity matters too. A steady stream of recent reviews signals an active, operating business. A burst of 50 reviews in one week followed by silence for six months looks unnatural and can trigger Google's spam filters.

## Building Local Citations and Backlinks That Move Rankings

Local citations are online mentions of your business's name, address, and phone number on directories, websites, and platforms outside your own site. Combined with local backlinks, citations form the off-site authority layer that supports your Google Maps ranking and local pack visibility.

Structured citations appear in business directories with standardized data fields — Yelp, Yellow Pages, Healthgrades (for medical), Avvo (for legal), TripAdvisor (for hospitality). Unstructured citations are mentions in blog posts, news articles, event pages, or forum threads where your NAP data appears but not in a formal directory format. Both types contribute to prominence, though structured citations tend to carry more consistent weight because Google can parse the data cleanly.

For local backlinks, you need a robust quality link building strategy. Instead of chasing general web authority, the focus should be on hyper-local relevance. The strongest sources are:

- Local business associations and chambers of commerce — these links carry significant local trust because they're editorially granted by organizations rooted in your community.
- Community sponsorships and event pages from youth sports teams, local 5K runs, or charity events. These are often easy to earn and hard for competitors to replicate.
- Local media via targeted PR platforms or HARO/Connectively pitching, where you offer expert quotes to regional journalists. One mention in a local newspaper's website can outweigh dozens of generic directory links.
- Partnership pages from complementary non-competitive businesses (e.g., a real estate agent linking to a preferred home inspector). These signal real-world relationships that Google values.

### Top Citation Sources and How to Audit Existing Listings

Priority directories depend on your industry. A healthcare practice needs Healthgrades, Vitals, and WebMD listings. A restaurant needs Yelp, TripAdvisor, and OpenTable. Every business — regardless of vertical — needs Google Business Profile, Apple Maps, Bing Places, Facebook, and the Better Business Bureau as baseline citations. These are the sources Google checks first when cross-referencing your business data.

Auditing existing citations means searching for your business name and phone number across directories and checking for inconsistencies. For businesses with 10+ locations, manual auditing isn't realistic. Citation management platforms like BrightLocal or Moz Local allow bulk CSV upload and cross-directory synchronization through APIs, reducing per-listing correction from hours to minutes. Even for a single location, running a citation audit once a quarter catches problems before they compound.

⚠️ Important: Duplicate or conflicting NAP listings are one of the most common — and most damaging — local SEO mistakes. When a business changes its address or phone number without updating all directories, the old data persists and creates conflicting signals. Audit your citations immediately after any address, phone, or business name change. Don't wait for rankings to drop before you notice the problem.

## On-Page Local SEO: Optimizing Your Website for Geo-Targeted Queries

On-page local SEO means structuring your website's content and metadata so that Google can match your pages to location-specific searches. Applying rigorous on-page SEO methods covers local keyword research, title tags and meta descriptions with location signals, dedicated location pages, and mobile optimization. Mobile optimization is non-negotiable — most "near me" searches happen on phones, and a clunky mobile experience kills conversions before they start.

Google uses mobile-first indexing, meaning the mobile version of your site is what gets crawled and ranked. Applying robust page speed optimization ensures that when high-intent searchers tap your listing, they don't bounce due to lag. If your site loads slowly on mobile, has unresponsive elements, or hides content behind tabs that don't render properly, your local rankings will suffer regardless of how well your GBP is optimized. I've seen sites with perfect profiles lose Map Pack positions because their landing pages took 6+ seconds to load on 4G connections.

### Local Keyword Research and Intent Mapping

Local keyword research identifies the geo-modified queries your customers use when searching for your services. The structure is typically [service] + [location modifier] — "emergency plumber Chicago," "family dentist in Scottsdale," "HVAC repair near me."

The process:

1. List your core services. Each service becomes a keyword stem.
2. Add location modifiers. City, neighborhood, county, "near me," and "near [landmark]" variations.
3. Check search intent. Map each keyword to the correct page type based on intent — is the searcher comparing options, ready to hire, or just gathering information?
4. Use keyword research tools to validate volume and difficulty. Tools like Semrush or Ahrefs surface "People Also Ask" data that reveal additional local intent patterns you might miss otherwise.
5. Map keywords to pages. Each primary keyword targets one page. Don't optimize five pages for the same "plumber in Austin" query — consolidate. Competing with yourself is a waste of crawl budget and link equity.

### Location Pages and Service-Area Page Structure

Location pages are dedicated pages built for each geographic area your business serves. They're essential for multi-location businesses and service-area businesses that operate across multiple cities without storefronts in each one.

The key rule: each location page must contain unique, substantive content. Thin location pages that differ only in the city name swapped into a template are a well-documented cause of ranking suppression. Google has seen this pattern thousands of times, and it doesn't reward it. Each page needs:

- Unique introduction referencing the specific area — mention neighborhoods, landmarks, or local context that proves you actually know the market.
- Service descriptions tailored to that location's demand. What customers in Miami need from an HVAC company differs from what customers in Minneapolis need.
- Local testimonials or case study references from clients in that area.
- Embedded Google Map for that location.
- LocalBusiness schema markup with the correct address, phone, and service area.

Schema markup for local businesses should include — at minimum —`@type: LocalBusiness`(or the most specific subtype, such as`Dentist` or`LegalService`),`name`,`address`,`telephone`,`openingHours`,`geo` coordinates, and`areaServed` for service-area businesses. This structured data helps Google connect your page content to its local knowledge graph, which feeds both the Map Pack and AI Overview source selection.

Hire a local SEO agency when the work exceeds your team's capacity or expertise — typically when you manage multiple locations, operate in a competitive metro area, or lack the time to maintain GBP activity, citation accuracy, and content production simultaneously. DIY local SEO works for single-location businesses with moderate competition and an owner willing to invest 5–10 hours per month. Beyond that threshold, the math usually favors hiring help.

### Signs You've Outgrown DIY Local SEO

- You manage 3+ physical locations and your NAP data is falling out of sync across directories.
- Your competitor — who has fewer and worse reviews — consistently beats you in the Map Pack. Something structural is off.
- Your in-house marketing lead is spending hours on manual directory updates instead of strategic outreach and growth work.

What separates a competent local SEO company from one that will waste your budget:

- Specific deliverables. The proposal should list exactly what the agency will do each month — GBP optimization, citation building and correction, review strategy implementation, content creation for location pages, and reporting. Vague "local SEO services" without itemization is a red flag.
- Reporting tied to business outcomes. Rankings and impressions matter, but the report should connect to calls, direction requests, website visits from GBP, and (where trackable) leads or conversions. If the agency can't explain how their work translates to business results, the reporting won't help you make decisions.
- Case studies with specifics. Ask for examples from your industry or a similar one. Look for before-and-after data: Map Pack visibility changes, local organic traffic growth, review count trajectory. Claims like "we increased traffic by 200%" without context — no industry, no timeframe, no baseline — are meaningless.
- No guaranteed rankings. Google's documentation explicitly warns against SEO providers that guarantee specific positions. An honest local SEO agency sets realistic timelines and benchmarks, not promises they can't control.

### How Long Does It Take to See Results from Local SEO?

Most businesses see measurable movement in local rankings within 3–6 months of consistent optimization. The timeline depends on competition level, the starting state of your GBP and citations, and how many ranking factors need correction.

Factors that accelerate progress: an already-verified GBP listing, clean NAP across directories, an established domain with some authority, and a steady flow of genuine customer reviews. Factors that slow things down: a brand-new listing, competitive metro areas with entrenched competitors, significant technical debt on the website, and a history of spam or policy violations on the profile.

Expect the first 4–8 weeks to be foundational — audit, GBP completion, citation corrections, on-page fixes. Ranking movement typically becomes visible in months 2–4, with compounding gains through months 4–6 as reviews accumulate and citation authority consolidates. Patience isn't optional here — it's part of the strategy.

### How Much Does Local SEO Cost?

Pricing varies significantly depending on whether you take a DIY approach or hire a provider. Investing in software like Whitespark or BrightLocal will run you between $30 and $100 per month. If you hire a professional US-based local SEO agency, retainers typically range between $1,000 and $3,500 monthly per location. Enterprise organizations pushing volume across dozens of zip codes may enter custom tier plans up to $15,000+ monthly. The right spend depends on your competitive landscape and how many locations you're managing — not on what sounds affordable in the abstract.

### How Can I Measure ROI From Local SEO?

To accurately measure ROI on SEO at the local level, don't look solely at raw rankings. Tag your GBP website link with UTM parameters so Google Analytics separates Google Maps traffic from standard organic traffic. Then use call tracking tools (like CallRail) on your GBP page and location pages to directly tie phone inquiries back to the local campaign. Without this tracking layer, you're guessing — and guessing doesn't help you justify the budget to your CFO or business partner.

### How Do AI Overviews and SGE Affect Local Search in 2026?

AI Overviews (the feature formerly branded as Search Generative Experience) appear above traditional search results for many queries, but their impact on local pack visibility is more nuanced than the headlines suggest. As of 2026, local pack results continue to appear prominently for queries with clear local intent — Google has not replaced the Map Pack with AI-generated answers for "near me" or service-area queries.

The primary concern is click-through rate compression. When an AI Overview answers an informational question (e.g., "how much does a roof replacement cost"), fewer users scroll to the organic results below. But for transactional local queries — "roofer near me," "emergency dentist open now" — the local pack remains the primary click target because the user needs to contact a specific business, not read a synthesized answer.

Local SEO in 2026 is being reshaped by heavier weighting on Google Business Profile (GBP) completeness and fresh reviews, alongside AI Overviews increasingly co‑existing with Local Packs. The strongest, consistent levers across sources are GBP optimization, on‑page/local page relevance, reviews (with recency/velocity upweighted), link authority, and behavioral/engagement, with AI Search altering how and where local visibility is won. ## Key Findings
1) Map Pack rankings in 2026 are driven by six signal groups; among the named groups and weights: GBP signals (32%), on‑page signals (19%), review signals (16%), link signals (15%), plus behavioral signals noted among the remaining groups. [1]

2) GBP completeness is a stronger ranking lever after the March 2026 core update; incomplete GBPs saw an average 18% local rank drop. [2]

3) Visual/content completeness matters: GBP photo completion was associated with a 67% impact (as reported by the source). [2]

4) Review recency/velocity carries substantially more weight post‑update: a 2.3x increase in the weight of review recency was reported. [2]

5) AI is changing local discovery: 43% of Local Packs appear with AI Overviews, and strategy guides explicitly integrate AI Search and AI‑generated answers into local visibility planning. [2][3][7]

6) Engagement/behavioral signals are ranking inputs; data‑backed guidance emphasizes optimizing GBP, reviews, and engagement to dominate local search. [1][8]

7) On‑page/local landing page relevance remains a core pillar (within the 19% on‑page share) in 2026 playbooks for Maps and Local Pack performance. [1][3][6]
